title: Where Names Live
content:
What problem does this solve?
As programs grow, the same name can appear in different places. A name created inside a function is local to that call; parameters are local names supplied by the caller. A function can read a global name, but depending on hidden global state makes behavior harder to understand and test. Assigning to a name inside a function normally makes that name local; reading it first can raise UnboundLocalError.

Previously in your program
You passed values into functions and returned results. You updated values in nested structures. Now you’ll make inputs and outputs explicit instead of changing module-level names from inside a function.

Basic syntax
  route = "north"

  def choose_route():
      route = "south"
      return route

  print(choose_route())
  print(route)

What actually happens
When Python sees an assignment to a name inside a function, that name is treated as local in the whole function body unless declared global. Reading a local before it is assigned raises UnboundLocalError.

When this is useful
Passing values in and returning results out makes a function’s behavior clear and easier to test. Use a global only when the whole program truly owns that single piece of state.
concepts: Names assigned inside a function are local to that call
Parameters are local names given by the caller
Reading a global can work, but hidden dependencies make tests fragile
Assignment creates a local; reading it first can raise UnboundLocalError
global exists but is not the pattern in this lesson

examples.title: Return value versus outer name
examples.code:
signal = "dim"

def calibrate():
    signal = "bright"
    return signal

print(calibrate())
print(signal)
examples.explanation: calibrate() returns the local value bright, while the outer signal remains dim.

common_mistakes: Relying on a hidden global instead of passing a parameter
Assigning to a name inside a function and expecting the module variable to change
Reading a would-be local before assigning it, which raises UnboundLocalError

exercises.title: The outer name stays the same
exercises.code_to_predict:
status = "waiting"

def prepare():
    status = "ready"
    return status

prepare()
print(status)
hints: Names assigned inside a function are local to that function.
prepare() returns "ready", but the outer status was not changed.

exercises.title: Make the dependency explicit
exercises.prompt: A helper must calculate a new supply count. Which design is clearest and easiest to test?
choices: Read and change a hidden global supplies variable.
Receive supplies as a parameter and return the new count.
Print the new count without returning it.
exercises.success_message: Yes — explicit input and a returned output make the helper easy to understand and test.
exercises.failure_message: Prefer passing values in and returning a result. Hidden globals or print-only helpers make behavior harder to reuse.
hints: Think about how you would test the helper in isolation.
Printing does not give other code a value to use.
Prefer a parameter for input and a return value for output.

exercises.title: Repair the hidden dependency
exercises.prompt: Refactor to use a parameter and return one less, leaving the module-level supplies unchanged.
exercises.starter_code:
supplies = 3

def use_supply():
    supplies = supplies - 1
    return supplies

print(use_supply())
hints: Subtract 1 from that parameter and return the result.
Call use_supply(3) at the bottom. Do not change the outer supplies.

tests.name: use_supply
tests.message: Define use_supply(supplies) so the value comes from the caller.
After your repair, the demonstration should print 2.

tests.name: supplies
tests.message: Do not mutate the module-level supplies — it must remain 3.

exercises.title: Apply damage explicitly
exercises.prompt: Write apply_damage(health, hit) that returns health - hit.

tests.message: Zero damage should leave health unchanged.
Health can become negative when hit is larger.
Do not hardcode — apply the subtraction to the given numbers.

exercises.title: Local party report
exercises.prompt:
Return a report built only from the parameter and local names.

Return exactly:
{
  "member_count": len(party),
  "total_health": ...,
}

Loop over each nested member record and total its "health" locally. The global total_health must remain 999.
exercises.starter_code:
total_health = 999

def party_report(party):
    # Build the report from the parameter and local names.
    pass
hints: Start total at 0 inside the function.
Loop over each member and add member["health"].
Return the dictionary with exactly the two requested keys.

tests.message: Use a for loop inside party_report to total member health.
Do not hardcode — calculate from the given records.

tests.name: total_health
tests.message: Do not change the module-level total_health — it must remain 999.
